paper.title: Contextual Bandit Learning with Predictable Rewards

settings.name_in_paper: Contextual bandit with realizable finite regressor class
unmapped: Realizability: a known finite regressor class F (|F| = N) contains f* with E[r(a)|x] = f*(x,a); policy class is induced Pi_F (argmax policies)
Learner knows the context distribution D(x) (removable via sample-based constraint, sketched in Section 7)
Learner knows the regressor class F
settings.definition_quote: At each round $t$, nature picks a context $x_t \in \X$ and a reward function $r_t: \A \to [0, 1]$ sampled i.i.d.\ in each round, according to a fixed distribution $D(x,r)$. We assume that $D(x)$ is known ... We are given a function class $F:\X\times\A\to [0,1]$ with $|F| = N$... There exists a function $f^* \in F$ such that $\E_{r\vert x}[r(a)] = f^*(x, a)$

settings.name_in_paper: Contextual bandit with realizable finite regressor class (lower bound)
unmapped: Realizability with a finite regressor class F of cardinality at most N; learner may know F and the (uniform) context distribution
settings.definition_quote: there exists a function class $F$ of cardinality at most $N$ and a distribution $D(x,r)$ for which the realizability assumption holds

conditions: context distribution D(x) known to the learner
tuning: delta_t = delta/(2 N t^3 log2 t)

source.label: thm:regret
source.quote: For all sets of regressors $F$ with $|F|=N$ and all distributions $D(x,r)$, with probability $1 - \delta $, the regret of Regressor Elimination is $\order(\sqrt{KT\ln(NT/\delta)})$.

results.notes: Regret defined via f* (means) along the realized contexts/actions; bound holds w.p. 1-delta. Computational complexity not addressed by the paper.

symbols.N_exp: cardinality bound N on the regressor class

conditions: hard instance: M = floor(ln N/ln K) uniform contexts, Bernoulli rewards with means 1/2 or 1/2+eps

source.label: thm:lb
source.quote: For every $N$ and $K$ such that $\ln N/\ln K \leq T$, and every algorithm $\algo$, there exists a function class $F$ of cardinality at most $N$ and a distribution $D(x,r)$ for which the realizability assumption holds, but the expected regret of $\algo$ is $\Omega(\sqrt{KT\ln N/\ln K})$.

results.notes: Expected regret with regret defined through f* means, hence pseudo_regret.

conditions: applies to algorithms working with the policy set Pi_F rather than the regressors

source.quote: For any algorithm $\algo$ working with a set of policies (rather than regressors), there exists a set of regressors $F$ and a distribution $D$ satisfying the realizability assumption such that the regret of $\algo$ using the set $\Pi_F$ is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{TK \ln N})$, but the expected regret of Regressor Elimination using $F$ is at most $\order\bigParens{\ln(N/\delta)}$.

results.notes: Derived from Theorem 5.1; Omega_tilde hides the ln K factor. Regret type not specified in statement (proof uses expected regret).

conditions: specially constructed regressor class F (with Pi_F equal to a given policy class containing the optimal policy) in which every non-optimal regressor has squared error gap >= 1/20 everywhere
tuning: delta_t = delta/(2 N t^3 log2 t)

source.quote: ...but the expected regret of Regressor Elimination using $F$ is at most $\order\bigParens{\ln(N/\delta)}$.

results.notes: Statement says 'expected regret' but the bound depends on delta and the proof is a high-probability argument (all suboptimal regressors eliminated within 10^6 ln(N/delta) rounds). Lemma 6.1 (lem:regressor-advice) states the same bound for any D and policy set; not recorded separately.
